worksheets.title: Data Collection, Summary Statistics and Outliers

fluency_questions.prompt: For the $9$ ordered scores $6, 9, 11, x, 17, 20, 23, 26, y$, given that the median is $17$ and the range is $25$:

parts.label: a
parts.question: Find the value of $y$

parts.label: b
parts.question: Given the mean of all $9$ scores is $17.5$, find $x$

parts.label: c
parts.question: Find the lower quartile $Q_1$ and upper quartile $Q_3$

parts.label: d
parts.question: Find the interquartile range ($\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$)

fluency_questions.prompt: A frequency table of scores $x \in \{10, 20, 30, 40, 50\}$ has frequencies $f = 4, 7, k, 5, 2$ respectively. Given the mean is $\bar{x} = 27.5$:

parts.label: a
parts.question: Write an expression for $\sum f$ and $\sum fx$ in terms of $k$

parts.label: b
parts.question: Solve $\dfrac{30k + 480}{k + 18} = 27.5$ to find the missing frequency $k$

parts.label: c
parts.question: State the modal score and the total number of scores $n$

parts.label: d
parts.question: Find the median score of the $24$ scores

fluency_questions.prompt: A dataset of $n = 15$ scores has mean $\bar{x} = 24$, median $M = 22$, range $R = 30$, and $\text{IQR} = 12$. Find the new mean, median, range, and $\text{IQR}$ after each linear transformation:

parts.label: a
parts.question: Every score is increased by $7$ ($y = x + 7$)

parts.label: b
parts.question: Every score is multiplied by $3$ ($y = 3x$)

parts.label: c
parts.question: Every score is transformed by $y = 2x - 5$

parts.label: d
parts.question: A $16$th score equal to $40$ is appended to the original $15$ scores (find new mean)

fluency_questions.prompt: For a dataset with five-number summary $\text{Min} = 4, Q_1 = 18, \text{Median} = 23, Q_3 = 26, \text{Max} = 41$, use the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ outlier fences:

parts.label: a
parts.question: Calculate the $\text{IQR}$

parts.label: b
parts.question: Find the lower fence $Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$

parts.label: c
parts.question: Find the upper fence $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$

parts.label: d
parts.question: Determine whether the minimum ($4$) and maximum ($41$) are formal outliers

application_questions.question: A logistics company in Brisbane operates three fleets of delivery vans: Fleet A ($12$ vans, mean daily distance $185\text{ km}$), Fleet B ($18$ vans, mean $210\text{ km}$), and Fleet C ($10$ vans). If the combined mean daily distance across all $40$ vans is $205\text{ km}$, find the mean daily distance of Fleet C.

Nine houses on a street in Fremantle have a mean value of $\$920\,000$ and a median value of $\$880\,000$. When the most expensive house (valued at $\$1\,480\,000$) is rezoned and removed from the residential list, find the new mean value of the remaining $8$ houses and explain why the new median must be less than or equal to $\$880\,000$.
application_questions.answer: New mean $= \$850\,000$ ($\dfrac{9 \times 920 - 1480}{8} = 850\text{k}$); the new median is the average of the $4$th and $5$th ordered prices, and since $x_4 \le x_5 = \$880\text{k}$, their average is $\le \$880\,000$.

application_questions.question: Five positive integers in strict ascending order $a < b < c < d < e$ have a median of $14$, a lower quartile $Q_1 = \frac{a+b}{2} = 8$, an upper quartile $Q_3 = \frac{d+e}{2} = 18$, a range of $14$, and a mean of $13.2$. Find all five integers.

When a data entry clerk accidentally records a student's exam score as $38$ instead of $83$, the calculated class mean is $68.2$, whereas the true class mean is $70.0$. Form an equation to find the number of students $n$ in the class.

reasoning_questions.question: Prove algebraically that for any dataset $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ with arithmetic mean $\bar{x} = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$, the sum of the signed deviations from the mean is always zero: $\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x}) = 0$.

Five positive integers written in ascending order $x_1 \le x_2 \le x_3 \le x_4 \le x_5$ have a unique mode of $12$, a median of $9$, and a mean of $8$. Find the maximum and minimum possible values of the smallest integer $x_1$.
reasoning_questions.answer: Since the median is $x_3 = 9$ and the unique mode is $12 > 9$, we must have $x_4 = x_5 = 12$ and $x_1 < x_2 < 9$ (so $12$ is the unique mode). Their sum is $5 \times 8 = 40$, so $x_1 + x_2 = 40 - (9 + 12 + 12) = 7$. Since $1 \le x_1 < x_2 \le 8$ and $x_2 \le 8 \implies x_1 = 7 - x_2$: the pairs $(x_1, x_2)$ are $(1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4)$, so $\min(x_1) = 1$ and $\max(x_1) = 3$.

worksheets.title: Sampling Methods, Data Displays, and Comparing Distributions

fluency_questions.prompt: A school of $1200$ students has year-level cohorts: Year 7 ($240$), Year 8 ($210$), Year 9 ($200$), Year 10 ($190$), Year 11 ($180$), and Year 12 ($180$). For a stratified random sample of size $n = 80$:

parts.label: a
parts.question: Find the sampling fraction $\dfrac{n}{N}$ as a simplified fraction

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the number of Year 7 and Year 8 students to include in the sample

parts.label: c
parts.question: Calculate the combined number of Senior students (Years 11 and 12) in the sample

parts.label: d
parts.question: If a systematic sample of $80$ students is selected from an alphabetical list of $1200$, what is the step interval $k$?

fluency_questions.prompt: A grouped frequency table of daily commuter travel times $t$ (minutes) has class intervals $0$–$<10$ (midpoint $5, f=6$), $10$–$<20$ (midpoint $15, f=14$), $20$–$<30$ (midpoint $25, f=18$), $30$–$<40$ (midpoint $35, f=8$), and $40$–$<50$ (midpoint $45, f=4$):

parts.label: a
parts.question: Find the total sample size $n = \sum f$ and modal class

parts.label: b
parts.question: Identify the class interval containing the median ($25.5$th score)

parts.label: c
parts.question: Estimate the sample mean $\bar{t} = \dfrac{\sum f \cdot m}{n}$ using class midpoints $m$

parts.label: d
parts.question: Find the percentage of commuters whose travel time is at least $30\text{ minutes}$

fluency_questions.prompt: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot (key $3 \mid 2 = 32$) compares battery life (hours) of Brand A ($18, 21, 24, 25, 27, 30, 32, 35, 38$) and Brand B ($12, 15, 19, 22, 23, 26, 28, 31, 64$):

parts.label: a
parts.question: Find the median and $\text{IQR}$ of Brand A

parts.label: b
parts.question: Find the median and $\text{IQR}$ of Brand B

parts.label: c
parts.question: Calculate the mean of Brand A and the mean of Brand B

parts.label: d
parts.question: Describe the shape of Brand A's distribution vs Brand B's distribution
parts.answer: Brand A is roughly symmetric; Brand B is positively skewed with a high outlier ($64$)

fluency_questions.prompt: Identify the primary type of sampling bias in each survey design and state how it affects the sample estimate:

parts.label: a
parts.question: An online newspaper asks readers to pay $\$1$ to vote in a poll on council rates
parts.answer: Voluntary response / self-selection bias (over-represents strongly opinionated readers)

parts.label: b
parts.question: Estimating average household income in Victoria by surveying shoppers in Toorak Village
parts.answer: Undercoverage / location bias (overestimates true statewide mean income)

parts.label: c
parts.question: Surveying gym members at $6{:}00\text{ am}$ on a Monday about weekly exercise hours
parts.answer: Selection / time-sampling bias (overestimates population exercise hours)

parts.label: d
parts.question: Asking employees face-to-face in front of their manager if they are satisfied with management
parts.answer: Response / social desirability bias (inflates reported satisfaction)

application_questions.question: A regional council in Gippsland surveys $150$ residents selected proportionally from three towns: Town A ($4500$ residents), Town B ($3000$ residents), and Town C ($1500$ residents). How many residents are sampled from each town, and if the sample means for weekly water usage are $1100\text{ L}$ (A), $950\text{ L}$ (B), and $800\text{ L}$ (C), what is the overall stratified sample mean?
application_questions.answer: Town A: $75$, Town B: $50$, Town C: $25$; overall stratified mean $= 1000\text{ L}$ ($\dfrac{75(1100) + 50(950) + 25(800)}{150} = 1000\text{ L}$)

application_questions.question: Two tomato cultivars are tested at an agricultural research station in Shepparton ($40$ plants each). Cultivar X has five-number summary $(1.2, 2.4, 2.8, 3.2, 4.1)\text{ kg}$ per plant, and Cultivar Y has $(0.8, 1.9, 3.1, 4.3, 6.5)\text{ kg}$ per plant. Compare their central tendency and consistency using medians and interquartile ranges, and recommend which cultivar suits a commercial canning factory requiring uniform yield.
application_questions.answer: Cultivar Y has a higher median ($3.1\text{ kg}$ vs $2.8\text{ kg}$), but Cultivar X has a much smaller $\text{IQR}$ ($0.8\text{ kg}$ vs $2.4\text{ kg}$), making Cultivar X far more consistent and predictable for commercial canning.

application_questions.question: A grouped frequency distribution of $40$ house rental prices (in $\$\text{/week}$) has intervals $400$–$<500$ ($f = 8$), $500$–$<600$ ($f = 15$), $600$–$<700$ ($f = 12$), and $700$–$<800$ ($f = 5$). Calculate the midpoint estimate of the mean rental price, and find the minimum and maximum possible values of the true mean of the $40$ ungrouped prices.
application_questions.answer: Midpoint mean estimate $= \$585$; Minimum possible mean $= \$535$ (all scores at lower class boundaries), Maximum possible mean (approaching upper boundaries) $< \$635$

application_questions.question: In a wildlife reserve, $60\%$ of wombats live in eucalypt forest (mean mass $28\text{ kg}$) and $40\%$ live in coastal heath (mean mass $23\text{ kg}$). A convenience sample of $50$ wombats caught near the ranger station consists of $15$ forest wombats and $35$ heath wombats; calculate the convenience sample mean and find the sampling bias (difference from the true population mean).
application_questions.answer: Convenience sample mean $= 24.5\text{ kg}$, true population mean $= 26.0\text{ kg}$; the convenience sample underestimates the true mean by $1.5\text{ kg}$ ($24.5 - 26.0 = -1.5\text{ kg}$).

reasoning_questions.question: Explain why for any strongly positively skewed distribution (such as Australian household wealth or house prices), the arithmetic mean $\bar{x}$ is pulled higher than the median $M$ ($\bar{x} > M$), and state why the ABS reports median and $\text{IQR}$ rather than mean and range for household income.
reasoning_questions.answer: Extreme high values in the long upper tail increase the total sum $\sum x_i$ proportionally to their magnitude (pulling $\bar{x}$ and the range up), whereas the median and $\text{IQR}$ depend only on the middle $50\%$ of ordered ranks and are resistant to extreme upper-tail values.

reasoning_questions.question: A population of $N$ items is divided into two strata of sizes $N_1$ and $N_2$ ($N_1 + N_2 = N$) with true stratum means $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$. Prove algebraically that if a stratified sample of size $n$ is chosen proportionally so $\dfrac{n_1}{n} = \dfrac{N_1}{N}$ and $\dfrac{n_2}{n} = \dfrac{N_2}{N}$, then the unweighted average of all $n$ sampled items automatically weights the two strata in the exact population proportions.
reasoning_questions.answer: The sample mean is $\bar{x} = \dfrac{n_1 \bar{x}_1 + n_2 \bar{x}_2}{n} = \left(\dfrac{n_1}{n}\right)\bar{x}_1 + \left(\dfrac{n_2}{n}\right)\bar{x}_2 = \left(\dfrac{N_1}{N}\right)\bar{x}_1 + \left(\dfrac{N_2}{N}\right)\bar{x}_2$, which matches the population mean formula $\mu = \left(\dfrac{N_1}{N}\right)\mu_1 + \left(\dfrac{N_2}{N}\right)\mu_2$.
